tagline: The reference transmitted-light method: the specimen is seen by how much light it absorbs or scatters out of the aperture of the objective.
principle: In brightfield the condenser floods the specimen with light and the objective collects both the light that passes undisturbed and the light diffracted by the specimen. Contrast arises only where the specimen changes the amplitude of the wave, by absorbing it (stains, pigments, chromophores) or by scattering it outside the objective aperture. Unstained cells are almost pure phase objects and are nearly invisible when the instrument is correctly set up.

Abbe's theory treats the specimen as a set of gratings. Each periodicity d diffracts light at angles given by sin θ = λ/d; the image of that periodicity is formed only if at least two diffraction orders (for example the zeroth and one first order) enter the objective. With oblique or full-aperture condenser illumination the smallest transferable period becomes d = λ/(NA_obj + NA_cond), so the condenser aperture is part of the resolving power, not just a brightness control.

Köhler illumination (August Köhler, 1893) images the lamp filament into the front focal plane (aperture plane) of the condenser and the field diaphragm into the specimen plane. Every point of the source then illuminates the whole field from a different angle, giving even illumination with no filament structure, a field diaphragm that sets the illuminated area (limiting stray light and heat), and a condenser aperture diaphragm that sets the illumination NA independently.

The microscope has two sets of conjugate planes. Field planes (field diaphragm, specimen, intermediate image, camera or retina) are where you see sharp images; aperture planes (lamp filament, condenser front focal plane, objective back focal plane, eyepoint) are where angles are encoded as positions. Most contrast methods (phase rings, DIC prisms, darkfield stops, oblique stops) are inserted in aperture planes, which is why understanding Köhler alignment underlies every other transmitted-light technique.

Closing the condenser aperture increases contrast and depth of field because it makes the illumination more spatially coherent, but it lowers resolution and produces diffraction fringes around edges. The usual compromise is a condenser aperture of about 70 to 80 percent of the objective NA. Colour (absorption) contrast obeys Beer-Lambert behaviour, so with careful flat-field correction brightfield can also be quantitative, as in densitometry of stained sections or haemoglobin absorption.

quiz.q: Walk me through setting up Köhler illumination and why each step matters.
quiz.a: Focus the specimen, close the field diaphragm and focus the condenser until the diaphragm edge is sharp (making the field diaphragm conjugate to the specimen), centre it and open it just beyond the field to limit stray light. Then set the condenser aperture to about 70-80% of the objective NA, viewed in the back focal plane, which balances resolution against contrast. The result is even illumination with independent control of illuminated area and illumination angle.

quiz.q: Why does the condenser NA affect resolution?
quiz.a: Under Abbe theory a periodic detail is resolved only if the objective captures at least two diffraction orders. Oblique illumination from a high-NA condenser tilts the zeroth order so that a first order at a larger angle can still enter, so the limit becomes λ/(NA_obj + NA_cond). With the condenser closed down to near zero NA the limit worsens to about λ/NA.

quiz.q: Why are unstained cells hard to see in brightfield, and what are the options?
quiz.a: They are phase objects: they change the phase of light by a fraction of a wavelength but absorb almost nothing, and the eye and cameras detect intensity only. Options are to stain them, to close the aperture or defocus (crude), or to use a method that converts phase into intensity: phase contrast, DIC, Hoffman modulation contrast, darkfield or quantitative phase imaging.

quiz.q: What is empty magnification?
quiz.a: Magnification beyond what the NA can resolve, roughly above 1000 × NA for visual work. The image gets bigger but no new detail appears. For cameras the analogous rule is Nyquist sampling: pixel size in the sample about half (2-2.3 times smaller than) the resolution.

tagline: Block the direct beam so that only light scattered by the specimen reaches the objective, giving bright objects on a black background.
principle: Darkfield illuminates the specimen with a hollow cone of light whose inner angle is larger than the acceptance angle of the objective. In the absence of a specimen no light enters the objective and the background is black. Any structure that scatters or diffracts light redirects some of it into the objective and appears bright.

In the Abbe picture the zeroth (undiffracted) order is excluded and the image is formed only from higher orders. This gives very high contrast for small or weakly scattering objects that are well below the resolution limit: a particle much smaller than the diffraction limit is not resolved, but it is detected as a diffraction-limited spot whose brightness reports its scattering cross-section.

For particles much smaller than the wavelength, Rayleigh scattering scales with the sixth power of diameter and the inverse fourth power of wavelength, so detection becomes rapidly harder for smaller particles. Metal nanoparticles scatter far more strongly near their plasmon resonance (around 520-550 nm for 40-80 nm gold), which is why gold beads are standard darkfield probes for single-molecule motor tracking.

Implementations are a central patch stop in a standard condenser for low NA objectives (NA up to about 0.65), a dry darkfield condenser, or an oil-immersion paraboloid or cardioid condenser (NA about 1.2-1.4) used with an objective whose NA is reduced below the condenser inner NA by an internal iris. Epi (reflected) darkfield uses a ring of light around a special objective for opaque samples.

Because the signal is pure scattered light against zero background, darkfield is extremely sensitive to dust, scratches and any out-of-focus scatterer, and images are not linear representations of structure: edges and small particles dominate while uniform areas look dark.

quiz.q: How can darkfield detect objects smaller than the resolution limit?
quiz.a: Detection and resolution are different. Darkfield removes the direct light, so even a tiny scatterer is seen against a black background as a diffraction-limited spot. You cannot resolve two such particles closer than about λ/(2NA), but you can detect and localise one if its scattered signal exceeds background and noise.

quiz.q: Why must the objective NA be smaller than the condenser NA?
quiz.a: The illumination is a hollow cone; if the objective acceptance cone overlapped it, direct light would enter and the background would no longer be dark. Oil darkfield condensers reach NA ~1.2-1.4, so high-NA objectives need an internal iris to stop down below that.

quiz.q: Why do people use gold rather than polystyrene beads for darkfield tracking?
quiz.a: Gold has a plasmon resonance that gives a much larger scattering cross-section at visible wavelengths, so smaller beads (40-80 nm) give enough photons for nm precision at high frame rates. Scattering drops as d⁶, so a small dielectric bead would be too dim.

quiz.q: What would you check first if the darkfield background is grey?
quiz.a: Condenser centring and height, oil contact and bubbles, whether the objective NA exceeds the condenser inner NA (close the iris), and dirt or excess particles in the sample.

tagline: Zernike's phase ring shifts and dims the undiffracted light so that invisible phase differences in the specimen become intensity differences.
principle: A thin unstained cell delays light passing through it relative to the surrounding medium by an optical path difference OPD = (n_specimen − n_medium) t. For typical cells this phase shift is a fraction of a wavelength, and because detectors record intensity, it is invisible in brightfield.

For a weak phase object the transmitted wave can be written as the undiffracted surround (S) wave plus a weak diffracted (D) wave that lags it by about a quarter wavelength (90 degrees). The two add almost in quadrature, so the resulting particle wave (P) has nearly the same amplitude as the background and there is little contrast.

Zernike's insight was to treat the two waves separately in the back focal plane of the objective, where the undiffracted light is concentrated into a small image of the condenser annulus while the diffracted light is spread across the pupil. A phase plate ring placed exactly there advances (or retards) the S wave by a further quarter wavelength, so S and D now interfere destructively or constructively, and attenuates S by typically 70-90 percent so that its amplitude is comparable to D. Phase differences thus become intensity differences.

In positive (dark) phase contrast, the common setting for cell biology, structures of higher refractive index than the surround appear dark on a grey background. Negative phase contrast gives the reverse. Contrast is approximately linear with OPD only for small phase shifts; thick or high-index objects (more than about a quarter wave) can show contrast reversal.

Because the phase ring has finite width, some diffracted light from low spatial frequencies also passes through the ring and is phase-shifted with the surround. This produces the characteristic bright halo around dark objects and shading-off, where the interior of large uniform objects fades to background intensity. These are intrinsic to the method and limit quantitative use.

quiz.q: Explain how the phase ring creates contrast.
quiz.a: For a weak phase object the diffracted wave is about 90° behind the undiffracted wave, so their sum hardly changes amplitude. The undiffracted light is concentrated in the back focal plane on the image of the condenser annulus, so a ring there can selectively advance it by another 90° and attenuate it. Now the diffracted and surround waves are in or out of phase and interfere to change intensity in proportion to the phase delay.

quiz.q: Where does the halo come from?
quiz.a: The phase ring has finite width, so low spatial frequency diffracted light from large structures falls on the ring and is shifted together with the surround. That light is then missing from the image of the object and reappears as a bright halo and shading-off. Narrower rings or apodized phase plates reduce it.

quiz.q: Phase contrast or DIC for cells in plastic flasks?
quiz.a: Phase contrast. DIC depends on polarized light and plastic is birefringent, which scrambles polarization and destroys DIC contrast. Phase contrast is insensitive to this and also tolerant of thick plastic with long working distance condensers.

quiz.q: Why can't you just read refractive index from a phase contrast image?
quiz.a: Intensity is only approximately linear in phase for small shifts, depends on ring attenuation, NA and alignment, and is corrupted by halo and shading-off. Quantitative phase methods such as digital holography or transport of intensity are needed for OPD or dry mass.

tagline: Two sheared, orthogonally polarized beams sample neighbouring points; their interference renders gradients of optical path as a shadow-cast relief.
principle: Differential interference contrast (Nomarski DIC) is a polarizing interferometer built into a microscope. A polarizer makes linearly polarized light at 45° to the axes of a Wollaston-type prism in the condenser. The prism splits it into two orthogonally polarized beams that are laterally displaced (sheared) by a distance smaller than the resolution limit, typically 100-200 nm at high NA.

The two beams pass through neighbouring points of the specimen. Where the optical path is uniform both are delayed equally; where the path changes with position (an edge, a gradient of thickness or refractive index) they acquire different delays. A second prism behind the objective recombines them, and an analyzer crossed with the polarizer lets them interfere.

The image intensity therefore depends on the difference in OPD across the shear, i.e. approximately the first derivative of optical path along the shear direction. Introducing a bias retardation (by sliding the objective prism or using a de Sénarmont compensator) shifts the background to grey so that positive and negative gradients appear brighter or darker, giving the familiar pseudo-3D shadow-cast look. The apparent relief is a gradient map, not topography.

Nomarski's modification places the interference plane of the prism outside the prism itself, so it can coincide with the objective back focal plane, which lies inside the objective barrel. Each objective therefore needs a matched prism. Because the condenser aperture can be opened fully, DIC uses the full NA, giving excellent lateral resolution and a shallow depth of field that provides a crude optical sectioning effect useful in thick embryos.

DIC is directional: features parallel to the shear give little contrast, so rotating the sample or using orientation-independent DIC helps. Because it relies on polarization, anything birefringent in the path (plastic dishes, strained optics, some lids) degrades the image.

quiz.q: Why does DIC not work in plastic dishes?
quiz.a: DIC relies on two orthogonally polarized beams being recombined and analysed. Polystyrene is birefringent from moulding stresses, so it alters the polarization of both beams in an uncontrolled way, which corrupts the interference and destroys contrast. Use glass bottoms and remove plastic lids.

quiz.q: What does DIC actually measure?
quiz.a: The difference in optical path between two points separated by the shear, i.e. approximately the gradient of OPD along the shear direction, plus a bias. So brightness reports slope, not height, and it is directional.

quiz.q: DIC versus phase contrast: when do you choose each?
quiz.a: DIC for high-resolution imaging on glass, thicker specimens (embryos, slices) and when halos would be a problem; it uses the full aperture and gives a shallow depth of field. Phase for routine work in plastic, thin cells, and robust, alignment-light imaging.

quiz.q: What is the role of the bias retardation?
quiz.a: With zero bias the background is black and both signs of gradient appear bright, so they cannot be distinguished. Shifting the prism adds a uniform retardation so the background is grey and opposite gradients go brighter or darker, which gives the shadow-cast appearance and linearises response near the operating point.

tagline: Between crossed polarizers only birefringent, ordered structures change the polarization and light up, revealing molecular order without labels.
principle: Polarized light microscopy places a polarizer before the specimen and an analyzer after it, crossed at 90° so that the background is dark. An isotropic specimen does not change polarization and stays dark. A birefringent specimen has two refractive indices for light polarized along its slow and fast axes; the two components travel at different speeds and emerge with a phase difference (retardance), so the light becomes elliptically polarized and part of it passes the analyzer.

Retardance Γ = (n_e − n_o) · t is the product of birefringence and thickness. Between crossed polarizers the transmitted intensity is I = I0 sin²(2θ) sin²(πΓ/λ), where θ is the angle between the specimen's slow axis and the polarizer. Brightness is therefore maximal at 45° and zero when the axes are parallel to polarizer or analyzer (extinction positions); rotating the stage identifies the axis orientation.

In biology birefringence arises from ordered arrays of anisotropic molecules or from form birefringence of aligned rods in a medium of different index: collagen fibres, muscle A-bands (the A stands for anisotropic), the mitotic spindle, cellulose, starch grains, amyloid stained with Congo red, crystals such as urate and calcium pyrophosphate in gout and pseudogout diagnosis. Biological retardances are often tiny, a few nanometres for the spindle, so extinction quality and compensation matter.

Compensators (quarter-wave, full-wave red plate, Brace-Köhler, de Sénarmont) add a known retardance to measure the specimen's retardance and determine its sign (which axis is slow). The full-wave plate turns the background magenta, with specimens appearing blue or yellow depending on orientation relative to the slow axis of the plate.

Quantitative methods such as the LC-PolScope use liquid-crystal variable retarders to acquire several polarization states and compute, for every pixel, both retardance magnitude and slow-axis orientation, independent of specimen orientation, with sensitivity in the sub-nanometre range. Related fluorescence polarization approaches measure dipole orientation of labels.

quiz.q: Why does a birefringent object appear brightest at 45° between crossed polarizers?
quiz.a: The incident polarization must be split into two components along the slow and fast axes for retardance to change the polarization. At 0° or 90° all the light is along one axis and the polarization is unchanged, so it is extinguished. At 45° the two components are equal and the sin²(2θ) factor is maximal.

quiz.q: What gives biological birefringence?
quiz.a: Intrinsic birefringence from aligned anisotropic molecules and form birefringence from aligned rod-like structures in a medium of different refractive index. Examples are microtubule arrays in the spindle, actomyosin in muscle, collagen and cellulose.

quiz.q: How do you tell real specimen birefringence from optical artefacts?
quiz.a: Check extinction without the specimen, use strain-free optics, rotate the specimen and see whether the signal rotates with it, and use glass not plastic. Quantitative systems take a background image and subtract the instrument retardance.

quiz.q: Why does extinction get worse at high NA?
quiz.a: Rays at steep angles are rotated in polarization at curved lens surfaces and at oblique incidence (different Fresnel transmission for s and p), so the edge of the aperture leaks light between crossed polarizers. Rectifiers or LC compensation help.

tagline: Two separate optical paths view the specimen from slightly different angles, giving each eye its own image and a true 3D impression at low magnification.
principle: A stereomicroscope presents each eye with an image of the object seen from a slightly different direction, typically with a convergence angle of about 10-16 degrees. The brain fuses the two views into a 3D percept (stereopsis, the same principle as Wheatstone's stereoscope), which makes manipulation, dissection and sorting under the microscope practical.

There are two designs. In the Greenough design two complete, small, tilted compound microscopes share a stand. It is compact, cheap and has good depth perception, but each channel views the object obliquely, so the image planes are tilted relative to each other, creating keystone distortion, and adding accessories in the path is difficult.

In the common main objective (CMO) design a single large objective is shared by two parallel channels that use off-axis parts of it. The parallel beams in the infinity space allow zoom bodies, beam splitters, fluorescence illuminators and camera ports, and give flat, distortion-corrected images. Most research stereomicroscopes and fluorescence stereo or macro-zoom systems are CMO designs.

Numerical aperture is low (often 0.05-0.15, up to roughly 0.3 in high-end apochromatic stereo or macro-zoom systems), because each channel uses only part of the main objective aperture. Resolution is therefore a few micrometres at best but working distance (tens of mm) and depth of field are large. Zoom ratios of 6:1 to 20:1 cover magnifications from a few times to a few hundred times.

Illumination is chosen to suit the sample: reflected ring lights or gooseneck lights for opaque objects, transmitted brightfield or darkfield bases (oblique transmitted light gives relief in embryos), and epifluorescence through the main objective for screening transgenic animals.

quiz.q: Compare Greenough and common main objective stereomicroscopes.
quiz.a: Greenough uses two separate tilted objectives: compact, inexpensive, good depth, but tilted image planes give keystone distortion and accessories are hard to add. CMO shares one large objective with two parallel channels: allows zoom, cameras, fluorescence and is the research standard, at higher cost and with off-axis aberrations.

quiz.q: Why is fluorescence on a stereomicroscope so dim compared with a compound microscope?
quiz.a: Each channel uses only a part of the main objective aperture and NA is low, ~0.1. Collection efficiency scales roughly with NA², and epi-fluorescence brightness scales with NA⁴/M², so signal is far lower than with a 1.4 NA objective.

quiz.q: What determines depth of field and why does it matter for dissection?
quiz.a: Depth of field scales as λn/NA² plus a geometric term; at low NA it is tens to hundreds of micrometres, so a whole embryo surface is in focus while you work, which a high-NA objective could not provide.

tagline: Epi-illumination excites the whole field at once and a filter cube separates the Stokes-shifted fluorescence onto a camera.
principle: Fluorescence microscopy exploits the Stokes shift: a fluorophore absorbs at one wavelength and emits at a longer one, so excitation and emission can be separated with filters. In the epi-illumination geometry (Ploem 1967) the objective serves as both condenser and collector. A filter cube holds an excitation filter, a dichroic mirror that reflects excitation and transmits emission, and an emission filter that blocks residual excitation by many orders of magnitude.

The whole field is illuminated at once by an arc lamp, LED or laser and recorded in parallel on a camera (sCMOS, EMCCD or CCD). This makes widefield the most photon-efficient and fastest way to image thin samples: every emitted photon collected by the objective is used, and the excitation intensity per point is low, which reduces saturation and nonlinear photodamage.

The 3D point spread function of a widefield microscope has an hourglass shape: in-focus light is concentrated in the Airy disc, but out-of-focus light from planes above and below spreads over the image without decaying in total intensity. In the frequency domain the optical transfer function has a missing cone of axial frequencies around the kz axis, so widefield has no true optical sectioning; a uniform fluorescent layer gives the same total signal at every defocus.

Deconvolution reassigns out-of-focus light using a measured or calculated PSF. Because the image is a convolution of the object with the PSF plus noise, iterative constrained algorithms (e.g. Richardson-Lucy) can restore contrast and partially fill the missing cone for samples a few micrometres thick. Combined with a sensitive camera, deconvolution widefield remains competitive with confocal for thin, dim live samples.

Epi-fluorescence brightness scales steeply with objective NA (roughly as NA⁴/M² for the combined illumination intensity and collection efficiency), so a high-NA, lower-magnification objective is often the brightest choice. Image quality is governed by shot noise: SNR ≈ N/√(N + background + read noise terms), so background suppression and detector choice matter as much as optics.

quiz.q: Why does widefield fluorescence not provide optical sectioning?
quiz.a: The total out-of-focus light from a plane is conserved: a defocused plane spreads its light over a larger area but the integrated intensity at the detector does not drop. In the frequency domain, the widefield OTF has a missing cone along kz, so there is no axial contrast for laterally uniform structures.

quiz.q: When is widefield with deconvolution preferable to confocal?
quiz.a: For thin, dim, live samples where photon budget is the limit. Widefield collects all emitted photons with a high-QE camera and low peak intensity, while a confocal uses a PMT with lower QE and discards some in-focus light at the pinhole. Swedlow et al. 2002 showed better SNR for such samples.

quiz.q: How would you choose camera pixel size?
quiz.a: Sample at Nyquist: projected pixel size about resolution divided by 2-3. At NA 1.4 with ~230 nm resolution, ~65-100 nm pixels are fine; a 6.5 µm sCMOS pixel at 100× gives 65 nm. Coarser sampling loses resolution; finer wastes photons per pixel.

quiz.q: How do you check for bleed-through and chromatic aberration in a colocalisation experiment?
quiz.a: Image single-labelled controls in all channels to quantify bleed-through and use sequential acquisition or narrower filters if needed. Image multicolour sub-resolution beads to measure lateral and axial chromatic shifts and correct registration before calculating colocalisation.

tagline: Total internal reflection at the coverslip creates an evanescent field that excites only the ~100 nm next to the glass.
principle: When light travels from a high-index medium (glass, n1 ≈ 1.518) into a lower-index one (water or cytoplasm, n2 ≈ 1.33-1.38) at an angle larger than the critical angle θc = arcsin(n2/n1), it is totally reflected. The electromagnetic field does not stop abruptly at the interface: a non-propagating evanescent wave extends into the second medium with an intensity that decays exponentially, I(z) = I0 exp(−z/d).

The 1/e penetration depth is d = λ0 / (4π √(n1² sin²θ − n2²)). It depends on wavelength and angle but not polarization, and is typically 60-200 nm for visible light. Only fluorophores within this layer are excited, so background from the cell interior and medium is almost eliminated and the signal to background ratio is excellent; this is why TIRF is the workhorse for single-molecule imaging at membranes.

Two geometries exist. Prism-type TIRF couples the laser through a prism on the far side of the sample; it gives clean evanescent fields and a free angle choice but limits access. Objective-type (through-the-objective) TIRF focuses the laser at the edge of the back focal plane of a high-NA objective so that it leaves the objective at a steep angle. This requires NA > n2; with NA 1.45-1.49 objectives there is a narrow range of supercritical angles available for cells (n ≈ 1.38), and NA 1.65 objectives with special coverslips extend it.

Near the critical angle the intensity at the interface can be several times the incident intensity, and the evanescent field polarization depends on the incident polarization (s gives a field parallel to the interface; p has a component perpendicular to it), which can be exploited to probe dipole orientation and membrane topology.

In practice the excitation is not a perfect exponential: scattering from the cell and imperfections in the objective produce a weak propagating component and a long tail, and real penetration depths can be larger than the formula predicts. Interference fringes from the coherent laser and uneven illumination are common; spinning the beam around the back aperture (ring or 360° TIRF) averages these out.

quiz.q: Derive or state the TIRF penetration depth and what it depends on.
quiz.a: d = λ0/(4π √(n1² sin²θ − n2²)). It depends on wavelength, incidence angle and the two refractive indices, not on polarization. Near the critical angle d diverges; at steeper angles it approaches ~λ/(4π√(n1² − n2²)), typically 60-200 nm.

quiz.q: Why do you need an NA of at least ~1.45 for objective TIRF?
quiz.a: The light leaving the objective has an angle set by NA = n1 sin θ. To exceed the critical angle at the glass-cell interface you need n1 sin θ > n2 ≈ 1.33-1.38. With NA 1.45-1.49 you have a small range of supercritical angles; at lower NA you cannot reach TIRF.

quiz.q: How would you calibrate the TIRF angle and depth on a new system?
quiz.a: Measure the exit angle directly with a hemicylindrical prism or by projecting the beam onto a screen, or infer depth from the intensity of fluorescent beads at known heights, a tilted surface, or dye in a layer of known thickness. Compare against the calculated d and check for the drop in background as you pass the critical angle.

quiz.q: What are typical artefacts in TIRF images?
quiz.a: Interference fringes and uneven illumination, scattered propagating light giving background, intensity variations from cell-substrate distance being misread as concentration, and fluorescent contaminants on the glass. Ring TIRF, clean coverslips and careful controls address these.

quiz.q: TIRF or HILO for imaging transcription factors in the nucleus?

tagline: A laser beam refracted at a steep angle just below the critical angle forms a thin inclined sheet that illuminates deep inside cells with low background.
principle: Highly inclined and laminated optical sheet (HILO) microscopy uses the same objective-type setup as TIRF, but the laser is displaced in the back focal plane to an angle slightly smaller than the critical angle. Instead of being totally reflected, the beam refracts at the coverslip and travels through the sample at a large inclination, forming an oblique sheet of light.

If the beam is narrowed in the sample plane (by closing a field stop conjugate to the specimen), the illuminated slab is thin where it crosses the focal plane. Tokunaga and colleagues gave its thickness as dz ≈ R / tan θ, where R is the beam diameter in the sample and θ is the refraction angle in the sample. A small field (10-20 µm) at a steep angle gives a slab of a few micrometres, so out-of-focus excitation above and below the plane is greatly reduced compared with epi-illumination.

HILO thus trades field of view for contrast: a smaller illuminated region gives a thinner sheet. Because the sheet is inclined, only a strip of the field is exactly in the focal plane, and the rest is excited slightly above or below. The incident intensity is concentrated, which helps single-molecule detection inside cells.

The related terms variable-angle epifluorescence (VAEM), oblique illumination and near-TIRF describe the same family of geometries. HILO became the default for single-molecule tracking of nuclear factors, chromatin binding and cytoplasmic mRNA, because TIRF cannot reach beyond ~200 nm from the glass.

quiz.q: How does HILO differ from TIRF?
quiz.a: In TIRF the angle exceeds the critical angle and only an evanescent field ~100 nm deep excites the sample. In HILO the angle is just below critical, so the beam propagates as an inclined thin sheet through the cell, reaching the nucleus with reduced out-of-focus excitation.

quiz.q: What sets the thickness of the HILO sheet?
quiz.a: Approximately dz = R/tan θ: the illuminated diameter divided by the tangent of the refraction angle in the sample. A small field and steep angle give a thin sheet; a large field gives a thick one, so there is a direct trade-off.

quiz.q: What would you control for in a single-molecule tracking experiment by HILO?

tagline: A focused laser scans the sample point by point and a pinhole in the image plane rejects out-of-focus light, giving true optical sections.
principle: In a point-scanning confocal microscope a laser is focused to a diffraction-limited spot in the sample, and the emitted fluorescence is imaged back onto a pinhole that is conjugate to (confocal with) the illuminated spot. Light from the focal spot passes through the pinhole; light from above or below the focus is defocused at the pinhole plane and mostly blocked. A detector behind the pinhole records one value per position and the image is built up by scanning, usually with galvanometer mirrors.

The effective PSF is the product of the excitation PSF and the detection PSF (shifted by pinhole size). For a very small pinhole this squares the PSF, narrowing the lateral FWHM by up to about √2 relative to widefield and suppressing side lobes. In practice pinholes are set near 1 Airy unit (AU), where lateral resolution is essentially widefield-like but sectioning is strong; the gain from closing further is small and costs a lot of signal.

The key benefit is optical sectioning: the integrated signal from a uniform fluorescent plane falls off as roughly 1/z² away from focus, whereas in widefield it is constant. Thus the confocal OTF fills the missing cone, allowing clean 3D stacks of thick samples (tens to ~100 µm, beyond which scattering limits).

Pinhole size is expressed in Airy units: 1 AU is the diameter of the first dark ring of the Airy disc projected into the pinhole plane, 1.22 λ M / NA. At 1 AU about 84 percent of light from an in-focus point passes. Larger pinholes increase signal and section thickness; smaller pinholes improve sectioning and lateral resolution only marginally while the signal drops steeply.

Scanning serially means each point is illuminated briefly but intensely. Pixel dwell times of about 0.5-10 µs mean frame rates of ~1-5 fps for 512×512 with galvo scanners and ~30 fps with resonant scanners. High peak intensity can saturate fluorophores (ground-state depletion and triplet accumulation) and cause photobleaching and phototoxicity in the focal volume, while out-of-focus planes are still excited and bleached even though their light is rejected.

quiz.q: How does the pinhole give optical sectioning?
quiz.a: The pinhole is conjugate to the focal spot. Light from the focus is imaged to a point at the pinhole and passes. Light from planes above or below is defocused into a large spot at the pinhole plane and only a small fraction passes. The integrated signal from a defocused plane falls as ~1/z², whereas in widefield it is constant.

quiz.q: What is an Airy unit and what pinhole would you use?
quiz.a: 1 AU is the diameter of the Airy disc to its first minimum projected to the pinhole plane, 1.22λM/NA. Around 1 AU gives good sectioning while passing ~84% of in-focus light. Open to 1.5-2 AU for dim live samples; closing much below 1 AU gains little resolution but loses signal.

quiz.q: Does a confocal have better lateral resolution than widefield?
quiz.a: Theoretically up to √2 better with a very small pinhole, because the effective PSF is the product of excitation and detection PSFs. At 1 AU the gain is minimal; the main benefit is sectioning and contrast. Image scanning microscopy recovers the resolution gain without losing signal.

quiz.q: A user's confocal z-stacks look squashed in depth. Why?
quiz.a: Refractive index mismatch: an oil objective focusing into an aqueous sample causes focal shift, so the actual focal displacement is less than the stage step (roughly by n_sample/n_oil in the paraxial approximation), and the PSF is elongated and aberrated. Use a water or silicone objective or apply an axial scaling correction.

quiz.q: When would you advise a spinning disk instead?
quiz.a: For fast live imaging of moderately thin samples where photobleaching and speed matter: the spinning disk spreads excitation over many points with lower peak intensity and uses a high-QE camera, giving faster, gentler imaging. Point-scanning is better for thick samples (less pinhole crosstalk), flexible zoom, FRAP, FLIM, FCS and spectral work.

tagline: Thousands of pinholes on a rotating disk scan the sample in parallel, giving confocal sectioning at camera speeds with gentle illumination.
principle: A spinning-disk (Nipkow disk) confocal replaces the single pinhole and scanning mirrors with a disk carrying thousands of pinholes arranged in spirals. Each pinhole acts as a separate confocal system: it is imaged onto the sample as an excitation spot and the returning fluorescence passes back through the same pinhole. As the disk rotates, the spots sweep the whole field many times per camera exposure, and a camera records the confocal image directly.

Early tandem-scanning designs passed only a few percent of the illumination through the pinholes. The Yokogawa design adds a second disk of microlenses aligned to the pinholes that focuses the excitation into them, increasing throughput to tens of percent, with a dichroic placed between the two disks so that emission passing back through the pinholes is reflected to the camera.

Because many points are illuminated at once with modest intensity and the camera has high quantum efficiency (sCMOS, EMCCD), spinning-disk confocals are typically faster and gentler than point scanners for live cells, with lower peak intensities, less saturation and less photobleaching per useful photon.

Pinhole size is fixed, so its size in Airy units depends on objective magnification and NA: a 50 µm pinhole is close to 1 AU for a 100×/1.4 objective but corresponds to roughly 2 AU at 60×/1.4. The spacing between pinholes (pitch) sets the degree of crosstalk: in thick or densely labelled samples, out-of-focus light passes through neighbouring pinholes, adding background and reducing sectioning. Larger pitch (and smaller pinholes) reduce crosstalk at the cost of throughput.

Variants include disks with different pinhole sizes for different objectives, wider pitch disks for thick tissue, and optical photon-reassignment designs that add microlenses in the emission path to gain resolution (e.g. SoRa). Spinning-disk systems are the workhorse for live imaging of embryos, cells and organoids where speed and gentleness matter.

quiz.q: Why is a spinning disk gentler than a point scanner for live cells?
quiz.a: Excitation is spread over thousands of spots, so the peak intensity at each point is much lower for the same frame rate. This reduces fluorophore saturation and nonlinear photodamage. The camera also has higher QE than most PMTs, so fewer excitation photons are needed per detected photon.

quiz.q: What is pinhole crosstalk and when does it matter?
quiz.a: Out-of-focus light from a thick sample spreads at the pinhole plane and can pass through neighbouring pinholes, adding background that is not rejected. It worsens with sample thickness, labelling density and closer pinhole spacing. Wider pitch disks or point-scanning reduce it.

quiz.q: What does the microlens disk do?
quiz.a: It focuses the excitation into the pinholes, raising the fraction of laser light that reaches the sample from a few percent (the pinhole fill factor) to tens of percent, which makes laser-based spinning-disk confocal practical.

quiz.q: Why does sectioning depend on which objective you use?
quiz.a: The physical pinhole size is fixed, so its size in Airy units depends on M/NA. A pinhole near 1 AU at 100× is ~2 AU at 60×, giving thicker sections. Systems offer different disks to match objectives.

tagline: Replace the confocal pinhole with a small detector array and reassign each element's photons, gaining resolution without throwing light away.
principle: In a confocal microscope, a very small pinhole improves resolution up to √2 but rejects most of the light. Image scanning microscopy (ISM) replaces the single detector behind the pinhole with an array of detectors (or a camera) that records the full image of the emission spot at each scan position. Each detector element acts as a small, offset pinhole.

The effective PSF for a detector element offset by d is the product of the excitation PSF centred on the scan position and the detection PSF centred at d. For equal excitation and emission PSFs the product peaks halfway between them, at d/2. Pixel reassignment shifts each element's signal back by this amount (scaled by a factor near 0.5, adjusted for Stokes shift) and sums. All elements then contribute to a sharper image, giving roughly √2 better resolution with the signal of an open pinhole.

Sheppard proposed this in 1988; Müller and Enderlein demonstrated it with a camera in 2010. Zeiss Airyscan (2014) uses a 32-element GaAsP hexagonal detector behind a pinhole, combined with Wiener-type deconvolution of the reassigned data to approach about 1.7-fold improvement in lateral resolution and better SNR than a 1 AU confocal.

The reassignment can be done optically. In instant SIM and rescan confocal designs, the emission is rescanned onto the camera at twice the excitation scan amplitude (or contracted by microlens arrays), which is equivalent to shrinking each emission spot by a factor of two around its centre. Spinning-disk versions (e.g. SoRa) add emission microlenses to the disk for the same effect.

Further gains come from deconvolution (enhancing high frequencies, which are now transferred with better SNR) and from combining with other contrasts, e.g. SPAD arrays for ISM-FLIM. ISM preserves the confocal's sectioning and flexibility and works in thicker samples than structured illumination, though resolution gains degrade with scattering and aberrations.

quiz.q: Explain pixel reassignment in one minute.
quiz.a: In a scanned confocal, a detector element offset by d from the axis sees the product of the excitation PSF at the scan position and the detection PSF at d, which peaks about halfway between. Recording all elements and shifting each by d/2 before summing makes all of them contribute to a √2 sharper image, instead of discarding off-axis light with a small pinhole.

quiz.q: How does ISM differ from SIM?
quiz.a: Both encode high spatial frequencies using structured excitation, and ISM can be seen as SIM with point illumination. ISM keeps the pinhole and point scanning, so it has confocal sectioning and works deeper, while widefield SIM is faster for thin samples but more prone to reconstruction artefacts in thick, scattering samples.

tagline: Two (or three) near-infrared photons absorbed together excite fluorescence only at the focus, giving intrinsic sectioning hundreds of micrometres deep in scattering tissue.
principle: In two-photon excitation a fluorophore absorbs two photons simultaneously, each carrying about half the energy of a single-photon transition, so a dye normally excited at ~460 nm can be excited at ~920 nm. Maria Göppert-Mayer predicted the process in 1931; it was first observed after the laser became available (Kaiser and Garrett, 1961) and turned into a microscope by Denk, Strickler and Webb in 1990.

The probability of two-photon absorption scales with the square of the instantaneous intensity. Because intensity falls off as roughly 1/z² away from a focus in both directions, the excitation per plane falls rapidly and fluorescence is generated almost only within the focal volume (on the order of 0.1-1 femtolitre). Sectioning is therefore intrinsic: no pinhole is needed, and photobleaching and photodamage are also confined to the focus.

To get enough two-photon absorption without heating the sample, light is delivered in ultrashort pulses (~100-150 fs) at high repetition rate (~80 MHz) from mode-locked lasers (Ti:sapphire, tunable ~680-1080 nm, or fixed fibre lasers at ~920 and ~1040 nm, and optical parametric oscillators to ~1300 nm). For fixed average power, signal scales as 1/(pulse width × repetition rate). Two-photon cross-sections are expressed in Göppert-Mayer units (1 GM = 10⁻⁵⁰ cm⁴ s photon⁻¹).

Depth comes from two effects. Near-infrared light scatters less than visible light (scattering length in brain ~150-200 µm at 920 nm versus ~50 µm in the visible). And because all fluorescence comes from the focus, scattered emission photons still carry valid signal: non-descanned detectors placed close to the objective collect them over a large area. The depth limit is reached when the power needed at the surface generates out-of-focus background near the surface comparable to the focal signal, typically ~0.5-1 mm in mouse cortex.

Three-photon excitation (signal ∝ I³) at ~1300 or ~1700 nm, where water absorption and scattering are balanced, suppresses out-of-focus background further and reaches over 1 mm into brain, including the hippocampus through intact cortex, at lower repetition rates (~1-4 MHz) and higher pulse energies. Multiphoton lasers also excite intrinsic contrasts: second and third harmonic generation (collagen, myosin, lipid interfaces) and autofluorescence of NAD(P)H and flavins.

quiz.q: Why does two-photon excitation provide optical sectioning without a pinhole?
quiz.a: Excitation scales with intensity squared. Away from focus the beam spreads over an area ∝ z², so intensity falls as 1/z², I² as 1/z⁴, and the integrated excitation per plane as 1/z²; summed over all out-of-focus planes this converges, so essentially all fluorescence originates at the focus. Hence all detected photons, even scattered ones, can be attributed to the focal spot.

quiz.q: Why are femtosecond pulsed lasers required?
quiz.a: Two-photon absorption is weak; it needs very high instantaneous intensity. Concentrating the average power into ~100 fs pulses at ~80 MHz increases the peak intensity by ~10⁵ relative to CW at the same average power, enhancing signal by the same factor (since signal ∝ ⟨P⟩²/(τ f)), without heating.

quiz.q: What limits depth in two-photon microscopy?
quiz.a: Scattering attenuates ballistic excitation exponentially, so power must increase with depth. Eventually out-of-focus fluorescence from near the surface (where intensity is high) becomes comparable to focal signal, and heating limits power. Typically ~0.5-1 mm in cortex; three-photon and longer wavelengths extend this.

quiz.q: Why use non-descanned detection?
quiz.a: Emission photons scattered on the way out cannot pass back through the scan mirrors and pinhole, but they still come only from the focus. Collecting them with large-area detectors close to the objective gains a lot of signal in tissue.

quiz.q: What would you check if two-photon signal suddenly dropped?
quiz.a: Laser mode-locking and power, pulse dispersion compensation, beam alignment and back aperture filling, objective immersion water, detector gain and shutters, and sample health (bleaching, heating).

tagline: A thin sheet of light illuminates only the plane being imaged from the side, while a camera on an orthogonal objective records the whole plane at once.
principle: Light-sheet fluorescence microscopy (LSFM, SPIM) decouples illumination from detection. An illumination objective or cylindrical lens creates a thin sheet of light that enters the sample from the side, and a detection objective at 90 degrees images the illuminated plane onto a camera. Only the focal plane is excited, so there is no out-of-focus excitation, intrinsic optical sectioning, and the photodose per volume is orders of magnitude lower than confocal or widefield scanning of a stack.

The sheet is a focused Gaussian (or other) beam. Its waist w0 sets the thickness (~2w0) and its Rayleigh range sets the length over which it stays thin: x_R = π w0² n / λ. The usable field of view is about 2x_R, so thickness and field are coupled: doubling the field of view requires √2 thicker sheet. For example at 488 nm in water a 2 µm waist (4 µm thick) stays thin over ~70 µm, while a 4 µm waist covers ~270 µm.

Static sheets are made with a cylindrical lens (SPIM). Digital scanned light-sheet microscopy (DSLM) scans a focused round beam rapidly across the plane during the exposure, giving more uniform illumination, efficient use of laser power and the possibility of structured illumination. Bessel beams, lattices and axially swept sheets extend the field of view with thin sheets but bring side lobes or require synchronized cameras.

Absorption and scattering in the sample cause stripe (shadow) artefacts along the illumination direction. Remedies include pivoting the sheet in its plane (mSPIM), illuminating from two sides, and multiview acquisition with sample rotation followed by fusion and deconvolution, which also improves axial resolution by combining views with different PSF orientation.

Light-sheet systems are cameras-on-volume: they generate data at hundreds of MB/s (e.g. 2048×2048 16-bit at 100 fps is ~0.8 GB/s), so storage, compression and processing pipelines (registration, deskewing, fusion, segmentation and tracking) are integral to the method. Designs range from multi-view embryo imagers and cleared-tissue mesoscopes to inverted and open-top systems for standard sample formats.

quiz.q: Why is light-sheet microscopy so much gentler than confocal?
quiz.a: Only the plane being imaged is illuminated, and each plane is excited only when it is recorded. In confocal and widefield, every plane is excited for each slice acquired, so the whole volume receives N times the dose for an N-plane stack. Camera detection also has high QE.

quiz.q: What is the trade-off between sheet thickness and field of view?
quiz.a: For a Gaussian beam the Rayleigh range x_R = πw0²n/λ sets how far the sheet stays thin. Field ≈ 2x_R, so thickness grows with the square root of the field. A thin sheet for high axial resolution only covers a small field, which motivates Bessel, lattice and axially swept sheets.

quiz.q: What causes stripes in light-sheet images and how do you fix them?
quiz.a: Absorbing or scattering structures cast shadows along the illumination direction. Pivoting the sheet in-plane, illuminating from both sides, multiview acquisition with fusion, and post-processing destriping reduce them.

quiz.q: What infrastructure would you need to support a light-sheet in a core?
quiz.a: Fast storage (tens of TB, high bandwidth), compression, a processing workstation or cluster with GPU, software for registration, fusion, deconvolution and visualisation, and user training on sample mounting.

tagline: An optical lattice of interfering Bessel-like beams, dithered into a sheet, gives a thin, long and gentle light sheet for 3D subcellular imaging.
principle: Gaussian light sheets cannot be both thin (sub-micrometre) and long (tens of micrometres), because of the Rayleigh range trade-off. Bessel beams, formed by focusing an annulus in the back focal plane, are long and narrow but carry most of their energy in concentric side lobes; scanning them into a sheet gives strong out-of-focus excitation unless used with two-photon excitation or structured illumination (Planchon 2011, Gao 2012).

Lattice light-sheet microscopy (Chen et al. 2014) uses a coherent, two-dimensional optical lattice: a periodic interference pattern of many beams whose wavevectors lie on a narrow annulus in the pupil. A binary spatial light modulator creates the lattice pattern and an annular mask in a pupil plane filters it. By choosing the lattice and annulus (outer and inner NA), the side lobes of individual beams interfere destructively, confining energy in a thin sheet with weaker side lobes than a scanned Bessel beam.

The lattice is either dithered rapidly along the sheet plane to create a uniform sheet (dithered mode), or stepped in phase to perform structured illumination along one lateral direction (SIM mode), which extends resolution in that direction. Typical systems use a water-dipping excitation objective of NA ~0.65 and a detection objective of NA 1.1 at an angle, with the sample on a 5 mm coverslip tilted relative to the objectives.

Volumes are acquired by scanning the sample through the sheet (sample-scan mode) or scanning the sheet and detection focus. Because the scan direction is not perpendicular to the sheet in sample-scan mode, the data must be deskewed, then often deconvolved. Resolution is roughly isotropic at about 0.2-0.4 µm with very low photobleaching, allowing hundreds to thousands of volumes.

Adaptive optics lattice light-sheet (AO-LLSM, Liu et al. 2018) adds wavefront correction on both excitation and detection to image subcellular dynamics inside multicellular organisms. Later work showed that well-designed Gaussian or optimized lattices can perform similarly for many tasks; the thickness-length trade-off still exists, but lattices allow finer control of it. Commercial lattice systems are available (e.g. ZEISS Lattice Lightsheet 7).

quiz.q: What problem does a lattice light sheet solve?
quiz.a: Gaussian sheets cannot be thin and long at the same time. Bessel beams are long and thin but have strong side lobes. A 2D optical lattice from an annular pupil uses interference to suppress side lobes, giving thin sheets over usable fields of view with low out-of-focus excitation.

quiz.q: Why do lattice light-sheet datasets need to be deskewed?
quiz.a: In sample-scan mode the stage moves the sample along a direction that is not perpendicular to the sheet, so successive planes are laterally shifted. Deskewing applies a shear transform to restore true geometry before deconvolution and analysis.

quiz.q: What is the difference between dithered and SIM mode?
quiz.a: Dithered mode sweeps the lattice rapidly to create a uniform sheet with a single image per plane. SIM mode steps the lattice phase and acquires several images per plane to reconstruct higher resolution along one lateral direction, at the cost of more exposures.

quiz.q: What are common criticisms of lattice light-sheet?
quiz.a: Complexity and cost, side lobes, limited sample formats, and analyses suggesting that optimized Gaussian or simpler sheets can perform comparably for many tasks. Proponents point to the controlled trade-off and established biological results.

tagline: Launch a tilted light sheet through the same objective that collects the image, then use remote refocusing to image that oblique plane on a camera.
principle: Oblique-plane microscopy (OPM) gets light-sheet sectioning through a single high-NA objective, so it works with standard samples on coverslips, in dishes and multiwell plates. The illumination beam enters the edge of the objective pupil so it emerges as a sheet inclined at an angle (often ~30-45°) to the focal plane. The fluorescence from this tilted plane is collected by the same objective.

The tilted plane cannot be imaged directly onto a camera, because it is not perpendicular to the optical axis. OPM uses remote refocusing (Botcherby et al. 2007): a second objective (O2) forms an aberration-free 3D replica of the sample space when the total magnification between sample and remote space equals the ratio of refractive indices (n1/n2), making lateral and axial magnifications equal. A third objective (O3), tilted to match the sheet, images the oblique plane in the remote space onto the camera.

The tilt of O3 relative to O2 means only part of O2's emission cone enters O3, reducing effective detection NA and photon collection; this was the main limitation of early OPM. Solutions include tertiary objectives with immersion (water or a solid glass tip) that capture the tilted cone, giving high NA systems with ~0.3-0.4 µm lateral resolution.

Volumes are acquired by scanning the sheet across the sample with a galvanometer mirror placed in a pupil conjugate plane. In SCAPE (swept confocally-aligned planar excitation), the same mirror descans the returning emission so the imaged plane remains stationary on the camera, enabling very fast volumetric imaging (tens of volumes per second) of behaving organisms. Stage-scanning OPM gives large fields for imaging many cells or tissue sections.

Data are acquired in a skewed coordinate frame and must be deskewed and rotated. OPM complements lattice and conventional light-sheet: it trades some resolution and sheet quality for compatibility with conventional samples and high-throughput formats.

quiz.q: How does OPM produce a light-sheet with one objective?
quiz.a: The illumination beam is offset in the pupil so it leaves the objective tilted, forming an oblique sheet. The same objective collects fluorescence; remote refocusing with a second objective creates a 3D replica of the sample, and a third tilted objective images the oblique plane onto the camera.

quiz.q: Why must the magnification between sample and remote space equal n1/n2?
quiz.a: Only then are lateral and axial magnifications equal, so the intermediate 3D image is a scaled replica free of spherical aberration and the tilted plane can be imaged without distortion.

quiz.q: What limits OPM resolution?
quiz.a: The tilt between secondary and tertiary objectives truncates the emission cone, reducing detection NA, and the sheet must be formed with part of the pupil, limiting sheet thickness. Immersion tertiary objectives recover much of the NA.

quiz.q: When would you choose OPM over a conventional light-sheet?
quiz.a: When samples must stay in standard formats (dishes, multiwell plates, in vivo preparations) or when very high volume rates are needed with SCAPE-style scanning, accepting somewhat lower resolution.
